This is a kind of heterogeneity that no amount of seller-level covariate engineering reaches, because the thing that varies is the *week*, and it varies differently for each seller. Overall CATT accuracy, meanwhile, is a wash --- if anything slightly worse with the covariate than without. That is not a contradiction, and it is worth understanding rather than explaining away. The promotional channel contributes a standard deviation of only 0.032 to an effect whose own standard deviation is 0.109; the catalog-breadth heterogeneity does the rest, and both models already capture that. So the signal the covariate unlocks is smaller than the error either model carries from everything else, and buying the freedom to look for it costs a little variance. The moderation is recovered; the aggregate score cannot see it. The residual SD column is the other half of the picture, and there the covariate does pay. Promotions lift GMV directly, and a model with no way to see them has to leave that variation in the error term: the blind fit reports 0.302 against a true 0.28, while the covariate-aware fit reports 0.282. That is the prognostic channel being absorbed rather than the treatment channel being resolved --- which is exactly why the two arguments are separate, and why the covariate went into both forests here. The lesson generalizes. A time-varying covariate earns its place when the question is *whether the effect depends on it* --- which is a targeting question, and the one the slope column answers --- and not as a general accuracy upgrade. If the marketplace wants to know whether to time the rollout to its promotional calendar, the blind model says no and is wrong. If it wants the tightest possible estimate of each seller's average lift, the covariate does not help here, and a larger sample would help more. Three practical points. Give the covariate to whichever forest needs it --- prognostic for a cleaner baseline, treatment for effect moderation, both if both. It must be observed in every cell, including cells where `y` is `NA`, because it is an input rather than an outcome. And it must be passed to `predict.longbet()` as well, in the same order, since the fitted trees record which axis each split used. ### When the effect varies beyond what the covariates explain {#sec-longbet-unitre} There is an assumption buried in every effect this chapter has reported, and it is easy to miss because the model never states it: **a seller's treatment effect is whatever their covariates say it is.** Two sellers with the same catalog breadth, vertical, fulfillment status and lookback history get the same $\tau$, always. The DGP at the top of the chapter was built that way, so nothing has yet gone wrong. Reality is not usually so tidy. Two sellers alike on every recorded variable can still respond differently --- one has photographs the optimizer can improve and the other does not, one prices well and the other does not, and neither fact is in `x`. Write that as $$ \tau_i(S) = \underbrace{\nu(X_i, S)}_{\text{what the covariates explain}} + \underbrace{\delta_i}_{\text{what they do not},} $$ with $\delta_i$ a seller-level departure the model cannot predict but can, in principle, *detect* --- because seller $i$ contributes their own before-and-after contrast. Without somewhere to put $\delta_i$, a model has only one option: call it noise. The consequence is not a slightly worse point estimate. It is an interval that is confidently wrong. On a panel whose unit-level departures have standard deviation 0.25, fitting the model as this chapter has fitted it throughout gives a nominal 95% interval that covers **30%** of the time. At 0.15 it covers 46%. Those are not conservative intervals; they are broken ones, and nothing in the fit announces it. `longbet()` gained `treat_effect_re = TRUE` for this. It adds $\delta_i \cdot Z_{it}$ to the effect, with a half-Cauchy prior on the spread of the $\delta$'s, and identifies it from each unit's own pre/post contrast --- so it needs at least one untreated and one treated period per unit, which is exactly the condition @sec-longbet-baseline already warns about for $\gamma_i$. | true spread of $\delta$ | coverage without | coverage with | RMSE without | RMSE with | |---:|---:|---:|---:|---:| | 0.15 | 0.46 | **0.92** | 0.150 | 0.129 | | 0.25 | 0.30 | **0.91** | 0.247 | 0.173 | Coverage returns to nominal and the effects get sharper. The fitted $\delta$'s correlate around 0.7 with the true ones, and the estimated spread comes back near the truth --- 0.29 against 0.25. **It is off by default, and the reason is worth understanding rather than working around.** When there is no unit-level departure --- when the covariates really do explain everything, as in this chapter's own simulation --- turning it on costs about 30% in CATT RMSE, because several hundred unit effects that are truly zero still have to be estimated. That cost is not a tuning failure. Four prior scales spanning a factor of ten were tried, and all of them settled at an estimated spread near 0.07: with a handful of treated periods per seller, a $\delta$ of that size is simply not distinguishable from noise. It is a property of the data, not of the prior. So the decision is genuinely the analyst's, and the fit hands you the number to make it with. Run it once with `treat_effect_re = TRUE` and compare `fit$sigma_delta` --- the estimated spread of the unit departures --- against the spread of the effects themselves. If it is a meaningful fraction, the heterogeneity is real and the intervals need it. If it is a rounding error, switch it off and keep the precision. The asymmetry argues for checking: 30% wasted precision is an annoyance, and a 95% interval that covers 30% of the time is a wrong answer presented with confidence. ### More than one outcome at a time {#sec-longbet-multi} Everything so far has treated GMV as *the* outcome. Almost no real rollout is scored that way. The optimizer rewrites listings, and the product team cares about GMV, about whether sellers keep using the marketplace at all, about support load. The interesting question is rarely about one of these; it is about several at once --- **is this seller worth \$500 a year, given that the \$500 only pays back if they are still here to earn it?** Fitting one LongBet per outcome cannot answer that, and the reason is worth being precise about. Posterior draws from separate fits are independent *by construction*. Multiply the two marginal probabilities together and you have assumed the two effects are uncorrelated --- which is the very thing the question is asking about. `longbet_multi()` fits the outcomes in one sampler and ties their errors together. Outcome $m$ is fitted to an **orthogonalized** target, $$ \tilde y^{(m)}_{it} = y^{(m)}_{it} - \sum_{l g_cut & sup_d < s_cut) p_prod <- rowMeans(gmv_d > g_cut) * rowMeans(sup_d < s_cut) tibble( Seller = c("Broad catalog (>= 50 listings)", "Narrow catalog (< 50)"), `P(both) from joint draws` = c(mean(p_joint[trt & broad]), mean(p_joint[trt & !broad])), `P(both) as a product` = c(mean(p_prod[trt & broad]), mean(p_prod[trt & !broad])) ) %>% kable(digits = 3, caption = paste( "Probability that the optimizer raises a seller's GMV above the median", "lift without raising their support load above the median, by catalog", "breadth. The model recovers the shock correlation almost exactly --- 0.59 against a true 0.6, never having been told it --- and the joint probabilities still come out within 0.003 of simply multiplying the marginals. A large error correlation did *not* make the shortcut wrong. That is worth sitting with, because the intuition says otherwise. Multiplying marginals assumes the two *effects* are independent given the data, and whether that holds is a question about the effect posteriors, not about the errors. Here their correlation is 0.11: near enough to independent that the product is right. The reason is the same one @sec-longbet-multi opened with --- both effects are driven by catalog breadth, both forests have `log_listings`, and each finds the structure unaided --- so the shared shock never reaches the effects. The value of fitting jointly, then, is not that it always changes the answer. It is that it *tells you whether the answer needed changing*, and separate fits cannot: they assume independence and report the product with no way to check. Here the check passed. Where it would not pass is when the effects vary across units for reasons the covariates cannot reach, which is exactly the situation @sec-longbet-unitre is about --- unexplained unit-level heterogeneity is shared across outcomes in a way covariate-driven heterogeneity is not. **Correlated *errors* are not the same as correlated *effects*.** Two outcomes can share a strong cell-level shock and still have nearly independent effect posteriors, and that is what happened here: shocks correlated 0.6, effects correlated 0.11. The reason is worth following, because it decides when the shortcut is safe. Two effect posteriors correlate to the extent their *estimation errors* do, and an effect is estimated by pooling every treated cell for that seller. The shared shock averages out of that pool. With 3,000 sellers and 18 weeks there is a great deal of averaging, so almost nothing survives into the effect posteriors. On a smaller panel less averages away: the same data-generating process at 1,200 sellers over 15 weeks leaves the effect posteriors correlated around 0.35, and there the product of marginals is visibly wrong. So the gap between the joint probability and the product is not governed by how correlated the outcomes look. It is governed by how much estimation error they still share, which shrinks as the panel grows. Big panel, covariate-driven effects: multiply the marginals, you will be right. Short panel, or effects that vary for reasons the covariates cannot see: do not. ::: {.callout-important title="Fit jointly for the joint question, not for sharper effects"} It is worth being blunt about what this does and does not buy, because the obvious guess is wrong. **It does not estimate any single effect more accurately.** Orthogonalization genuinely shrinks the innovation variance --- on a controlled panel with shock correlation 0.8 the second outcome's residual SD fell from 0.499 to 0.307, against a theoretical floor of 0.30 --- and that is a large, real reduction. It does not translate into a better $\tau$. Compared against literally fitting a separate `longbet()` per outcome, over 12 replications in each of four conditions crossing correlated effects with correlated errors, the CATT RMSE differences ran from $-0.9\%$ to $+7.4\%$ and **not one was distinguishable from zero** (all $|t| < 1.3$). Whatever limits CATT accuracy here, it is not the part of the error the coupling removes. **What it buys is the joint posterior**, and separate fits cannot produce that at any sample size. That is the whole case for the feature. **One caveat with a diagnostic attached.** The residual one outcome conditions on is meant to be pure shock, but whatever of that outcome's *own* effect the forest has not yet fitted stays in it --- and when the two effects are correlated, subtracting it strips real signal from the next outcome. That leakage is a small-sample and short-sampler problem, and it is measurable: at $n = 700$ over 10 periods with 50 sweeps the joint fit was 16% worse than separate fits, at $n = 1200$ over 15 periods with 100 sweeps the gap was gone, and by $n = 2000$ with 150 sweeps it had turned slightly positive. The remedy is the sampler-length check of @sec-longbet-sampler: `att_stability()` flags an under-sampled fit, and an under-sampled fit is exactly the one that leaks. **One trap it avoids for you.** A probit's latent scale is fixed by the link, so its residual variance is pinned at 1 and orthogonalizing it makes the fit *worse* --- measurably, about 10% on effect RMSE. `longbet_multi()` therefore leaves binary outcomes un-orthogonalized: they share the sampler, so their draws stay paired for joint inference, but each is fitted exactly as it would be alone. ::: ### Operating characteristics {#sec-longbet-operating} @sec-longbet-scorecard scored three estimators on one dataset and warned that the "contained truth" column was not a coverage estimate. That warning is easy to write and easy to leave standing. The honest version costs a few minutes of compute: redraw the whole experiment many times and see how the estimators behave in repeated sampling, which is the only setting in which words like *unbiased* and *95% interval* mean anything. Each replication draws a fresh population of sellers, a fresh randomization into waves, fresh noise, and scores every estimator against **its own** realized truth. The data-generating process is the one from the top of the chapter --- same effect shapes, same seasonality, same non-parallel trends. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} N_REPS <- 40 # replications MC_N <- 1200 # sellers per replication (the headline fit uses 3000) MC_SWEEPS <- c(80, 200) # run the whole thing at two sampler lengths # (200 is what the headline fit uses) ``` ::: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} # One complete replication: simulate a rollout, fit all three estimators, and # score them against the truth for that draw. Deliberately smaller and coarser # than the headline fit -- see the note under the table. mc_replication <- function(seed, n = MC_N, sweeps = 80, trees = 25) { set.seed(seed) weeks_all <- c(week_base, week_study) Tn <- length(weeks_all) vertical <- sample(c("Apparel", "Home", "Electronics"), n, TRUE, c(.40, .35, .25)) fulfilled <- rbinom(n, 1, 0.45) listings <- pmax(1, round(exp(rnorm(n, log(35), 0.9)))) seller_sd <- rnorm(n) strata <- interaction(vertical, cut(listings, unique(quantile(listings, 0:3 / 3)), include.lowest = TRUE), fulfilled, drop = TRUE) deal <- function(k) sample(rep(c("W1", "W2", "W3", "W4", "Holdout"), diff(round(k * cumsum(c(0, .15, .15, .15, .15, .40)))))) wave <- character(n) for (st in levels(strata)) { ii <- which(strata == st); wave[ii] <- deal(length(ii)) } launch <- LAUNCH[wave] level_i <- 6.4 + .55 * seller_sd + .45 * log(listings / 35) + .25 * fulfilled + rnorm(n, 0, .35) drift_i <- .004 * seller_sd + c(Apparel = 0, Home = .002, Electronics = .008)[vertical] tmat <- matrix(rep(weeks_all, each = n), n, Tn) y0 <- matrix(level_i, n, Tn) + outer(drift_i, weeks_all, "*") + season(matrix(vertical, n, Tn), tmat) + matrix(rnorm(n * Tn, 0, .28), n, Tn) S <- tmat - matrix(launch, n, Tn) + 1 S[!is.finite(S) | S < 0] <- 0 S <- matrix(as.numeric(S), n, Tn) Z <- matrix(as.integer(S > 0), n, Tn) w_i <- plogis((log(listings) - log(50)) / 0.35) tau <- ifelse(S > 0, w_i * h_grow(S) + (1 - w_i) * h_fade(S), 0) y <- y0 + tau wb <- week_base - mean(week_base) x <- cbind(rowMeans(y[, week_base]), as.vector((y[, week_base] %*% wb) / sum(wb^2)), log(listings), fulfilled, as.integer(factor(vertical))) colnames(x) <- c("base_level", "base_slope", "log_listings", "fulfilled", "vertical") z_tr <- Z[, week_study] S_obs <- max(rowSums(z_tr)) truth <- event_time_truth(tau[, week_study], z_tr)[seq_len(S_obs)] f <- longbet(y = y[, week_study], x = x, x_trt = x, z = z_tr, t = week_study, pcat = 2, num_sweeps = sweeps, num_burnin = sweeps %/% 3, num_trees_pr = trees, num_trees_trt = trees, sig_knl = 1, lambda_knl = 2, random_intercept = TRUE, random_seed = seed, verbose = FALSE) a <- get_att(predict.longbet(f, x, x, z_tr, t = week_study, random_seed = seed)) # The fit and its posterior arrays are the bulk of the memory here, and at # the longer sampler length several workers holding one at once is enough to # get a worker killed. Nothing below needs them. rm(f); gc(verbose = FALSE) # The same two comparison estimators, rebuilt for this draw. pre <- 7:10 is_hold <- wave == "Holdout" dY <- y - rowMeans(y[, pre]); colnames(dY) <- weeks_all xdf <- as.data.frame(x) xdf$vertical <- factor(xdf$vertical) xdf$fulfilled <- factor(xdf$fulfilled) dY_adj <- dY for (cc in seq_len(ncol(dY))) { m <- lm(dY[is_hold, cc] ~ ., data = xdf[is_hold, , drop = FALSE]) dY_adj[, cc] <- dY[, cc] - predict(m, newdata = xdf) } did <- function(D) map_dfr(seq_len(S_obs), function(s) { ws <- c("W1", "W2", "W3", "W4") ws <- ws[LAUNCH[ws] + s - 1 <= max(week_study)] nt <- vapply(ws, function(w) sum(wave == w), integer(1)) ws <- ws[nt > 1]; nt <- nt[nt > 1]; aw <- nt / sum(nt) col <- match(as.integer(LAUNCH[ws] + s - 1), weeks_all) tm <- vapply(seq_along(ws), function(j) mean(D[wave == ws[j], col[j]]), numeric(1)) vm <- vapply(seq_along(ws), function(j) var(D[wave == ws[j], col[j]]) / nt[j], numeric(1)) hc <- as.vector(D[is_hold, col, drop = FALSE] %*% aw) est <- sum(aw * tm) - mean(hc) se <- sqrt(sum(aw^2 * vm) + var(hc) / sum(is_hold)) tibble(s = s, estimate = est, lower = est - 1.96 * se, upper = est + 1.96 * se) }) bind_rows( tibble(estimator = "LongBet", s = seq_len(S_obs), estimate = a$att[seq_len(S_obs)], lower = a$intervals[1, seq_len(S_obs)], upper = a$intervals[2, seq_len(S_obs)]), did(dY) %>% mutate(estimator = "DiD vs holdout"), did(dY_adj) %>% mutate(estimator = "DiD + covariate adjustment") ) %>% mutate(truth = truth[s], seed = seed) } # Sequential on purpose. Each replication holds a full posterior array, and # parallel workers were repeatedly killed for memory on a 16 GB machine at the # longer sampler length -- a slow chunk that finishes beats a fast one that # dies. It is cached, so the cost is paid once. mc <- map_dfr(MC_SWEEPS, function(sw) { map_dfr(1000 + seq_len(N_REPS), function(seed) mc_replication(seed, sweeps = sw)) %>% mutate(sweeps = sw) }) ``` ::: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} mc %>% # the two comparison estimators do not depend on the sampler, so report # them once rather than twice filter(estimator == "LongBet" | sweeps == max(MC_SWEEPS)) %>% mutate(Estimator = ifelse(estimator == "LongBet", paste0("LongBet (", sweeps, " sweeps)"), estimator)) %>% group_by(Estimator) %>% summarise(Bias = mean(estimate - truth), RMSE = sqrt(mean((estimate - truth)^2)), Coverage = mean(truth >= lower & truth <= upper), `Interval width` = mean(upper - lower), .groups = "drop") %>% arrange(RMSE) %>% mutate(Coverage = scales::percent(Coverage, 0.1)) %>% kable(digits = 4, caption = paste( N_REPS, "independent replications of the whole rollout, each scored", "against its own truth over", max(mc$s), "event times.", "Nominal coverage is 95%." )) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} Table: 40 independent replications of the whole rollout, each scored against its own truth over 14 event times. Nominal coverage is 95%. |Estimator | Bias| RMSE|Coverage | Interval width| |:--------------------------|-------:|------:|:--------|--------------:| |LongBet (200 sweeps) | -0.0019| 0.0123|95.2% | 0.0487| |LongBet (80 sweeps) | -0.0021| 0.0128|92.0% | 0.0458| |DiD + covariate adjustment | 0.0011| 0.0160|95.5% | 0.0649| |DiD vs holdout | 0.0006| 0.0163|98.6% | 0.0870| ::: ::: Three things, and the second is the one to take away. **All three estimators are unbiased.** Bias is two orders of magnitude below the effects being estimated. That is randomization doing its job, and it is the result that would have been alarming had it come out otherwise. **Coverage is a property of how long you run the sampler, not of the model.** At 80 sweeps LongBet's intervals cover 92.0% of the time against a nominal 95%. At 200 sweeps, on the same data-generating process and the same seeds, they cover 95.2%. Nothing about the panel changed. What changed is that the sampler had longer to explore, and XBART grows a fresh forest every sweep rather than walking one chain through tree space, so its posterior is an *approximation* whose quality is a function of how many sweeps you average over. Too few and you are looking at a slice of the posterior rather than the posterior, which is narrow for the same reason any under-explored posterior is narrow. Notice that the intervals barely widen --- 0.0458 to 0.0487 --- while RMSE improves by 4%. The extra sweeps buy coverage mostly by moving the *estimate* onto the truth, not by widening the band around it. That is the practical rule: **a sampler setting adequate for a point estimate can be inadequate for an interval**, and `att_stability()` (@sec-longbet-sampler) is how you tell without running forty replications: it reports the effective sweep count, and the two arms here are what calibrates it --- a median near 23 at 80 sweeps, where coverage is 92.0%, against a median near 42 at 200, where it is nominal. The package's default threshold sits between them for that reason, and it is a smoke alarm rather than a theorem: effective sweeps depend on the panel, so on data unlike this the number to read is the count itself, not the verdict. The headline fit in this chapter uses 200 sweeps, nearer the calibrated end than the 80 used here to keep forty replications affordable. **LongBet is more precise than either comparison, and the covariate-adjusted one is the best calibrated.** LongBet has the lowest RMSE and the narrowest intervals at both sampler lengths, and the ordering of widths reproduces the single realization in @sec-longbet-scorecard, so that comparison was not a lucky draw. The unadjusted difference-in-differences over-covers, at 98.6% --- its standard error is conservative here --- while the covariate-adjusted version lands closest to nominal. If what you need is an interval you can defend line by line, without a sampler-length caveat attached, that remains a real argument for the simpler estimator, and it costs one `lm()`. ::: {.callout-important title="What this changed about the chapter's own diagnosis"} An earlier draft of this section attributed the under-coverage to the serial correlation documented in @sec-longbet-serial: a design effect near 3, from within-seller dependence the likelihood does not represent, producing intervals computed as though weeks were independent. The story was tidy and it was wrong. A design effect is a property of the data, so it cannot be what more sweeps repaired --- and more sweeps repaired it, on the same panels. The serial correlation is real and still worth knowing about; it is not what drives this. Two other candidates were checked and can also be set aside. In a separate run not reproduced here --- 24 replications at 80 sweeps --- turning the unit random intercept off moved coverage from 89.3% to 89.0%, which is nothing, so $\gamma_i$ is not what is holding coverage up and a richer unit effect such as a random slope would not be aimed at the right target. And the estimand here is the *realized sample* ATT of the units actually drawn, computed by `event_time_truth()`, so there is no finite-population term the posterior is missing. ::: ::: {.callout-note title="What this does and does not establish"} These replications use 1200 sellers against 3000 in the headline fit. That is deliberate --- forty full-scale fits at two sampler lengths would dominate the build --- but it means the numbers describe the operating characteristics *of this configuration*, and a larger sample should do at least as well on bias and RMSE. It also remains one data-generating process, and one that this chapter chose to make a business point. Nothing here establishes how LongBet behaves in general. @wang2024longbet reports 94--98% coverage across 100 replications of a different design, which is consistent with what the longer sampler gives here. ::: ### Treatment has to stay on {#sec-longbet-absorbing} Everything above assumes **absorbing** treatment: a seller who launches stays launched. That is not a convention of the example, it is a requirement of the model, and it is worth being explicit about because the failure is not graceful. $\beta_S$ is a single trajectory indexed by time since adoption, and the index is computed once from a unit's first treated period and then counted forward. Nothing rereads $z$ afterwards. So if a unit is switched back off, the index keeps climbing, the model goes on applying an effect through the switched-off weeks, and the number it reports there is close to the full effect rather than zero. In one test panel whose true effect while off was exactly 0, it returned 0.49. As of `longbet` 0.5.2 a panel like that is rejected with an explanatory error rather than either crashing or answering. The temptation, once you have a panel model that handles staggered adoption, is to reach for it on a **switchback** --- the design where the same units are toggled on and off, used when there is no clean holdout because the units interfere with each other. Resist it, and not only for the implementation reason. The question a switchback is usually run to answer is how long the effect lingers after it is withdrawn, and *for whom*. That second half is a heterogeneity in the *trajectory itself* --- some units revert immediately, others keep the gain --- which is to say a $\beta$ that varies by unit. @sec-longbet-sampler is about the ridge between $\beta$ and $\nu$ when $\beta$ is one shared scalar per event time; asking $\nu$ to carry unit-level persistence on top of that is asking the two to separate along the direction they are least able to separate. Attempts to estimate it recover the ranking of units unreliably and the level not at all. For switchbacks, use randomization inference over the switching sequence, or a distributed-lag model that estimates the carryover decay directly. Both are assumption-lighter exactly where switchbacks are hard. ### Design notes for the experiment itself - **The event-time tail is thin.** In this rollout the last event time is reached by one wave only. Estimates and intervals at the far right of @fig-att rest on a quarter of the treated sample, and the Gaussian process extrapolation starts from exactly there. If the long-run effect is the decision-relevant quantity, launch the waves close together and run the study longer, rather than spreading the launches out. - **Randomize the launch order, and stratify it.** Letting the field team choose who goes first turns a clean experiment into an observational study with targeted selection --- the setting BCF and LongBet were built to survive, but survival is not the same as free precision. - **SUTVA does not come with randomization, and here it is the binding constraint.** Search results are a ranked list of fixed length. If the optimizer works by moving treated sellers up it, some of the measured lift is demand *taken from* holdout sellers rather than demand created. Every dollar figure in @sec-longbet-decision assumes it is created. In the zero-sum extreme the two policies come apart completely: targeting still pays, because it moves the ranking advantage to the sellers who monetize it best, but shipping to *everyone* returns the ranking to where it started and earns nothing at all --- while still costing \$500 a head. Total GMV rises only to the extent the optimizer brings in buyers who would not otherwise have transacted, or converts browsers who would have bounced. That is an empirical question, and the experiment as designed cannot answer it: you need to randomize at a level that contains the competition, such as category, geography, or marketplace, so that whole ranked lists are treated or untreated together. Seller-level randomization measures who wins the race; market-level randomization measures whether the race got faster. - **Serial correlation is still assumed away.** The random intercept handles the permanent part of within-unit dependence, which on this panel is all of it. A genuinely autoregressive error is untouched, and the fix is not a small one --- see @sec-longbet-limits. - **Used observationally, everything rests on $X$.** Outside an experiment, LongBet trades the parallel trends assumption for the assumption that $X_i$ contains every confounder of adoption timing and outcome. That is a different assumption, not a weaker one; it is only an improvement when you actually observe the drivers of adoption. ## Conclusion LongBet earns its place in a business setting by answering a question that neither a cross-sectional causal forest nor a classical panel estimator can: not *what is the effect*, but *what does the effect do over time, and to whom*. In this chapter the pooled average told a clean and completely misleading story --- a lift that gave back a third of its peak inside three months, the textbook signature of a novelty effect. The same model, asked one level down, found two populations moving in opposite directions: broad-catalog sellers on a compounding trajectory that showed no sign of turning down when the study ended, and narrow-catalog sellers whose bump was largely spent by the second month. Acting on that distinction was worth roughly half a million dollars a year in a 3,000-seller pilot, and no amount of extra sample would have surfaced it from an average. Four cautions are worth carrying forward. The randomization, not the model, is what makes the estimates credible: keep a simple difference-in-differences against the holdout in view as a check, and treat disagreement as a bug report. The credible intervals assume errors are independent across units *and* across time, and the residual diagnostic in @sec-longbet-limits shows how quietly that fails even when the errors really are independent. The forecast extrapolates one shared factor under a prior you choose, so it belongs in a sensitivity analysis rather than in the plan. And every dollar figure assumes the lift is demand created rather than demand moved off the holdout --- in a ranked marketplace that is the strongest assumption in the chapter, and no model can test it. Only a market-level randomization can. One habit generalizes past this model. Diagnose the quantity you are going to report, not the parameter that produces it: LongBet's shared factor drifts because it is identified only up to a scale it shares with the treatment forest, while the effect the two multiply out to sits still. ::: {.callout-tip} ## Learn more - @wang2024longbet LongBet: Heterogeneous Treatment Effect Estimation in Panel Data --- the method, its simulation study, and the forecasting extension. - @longbetpkg The `longbet` R package. - @hahn2020bayesian Bayesian regression tree models for causal inference --- the cross-sectional model LongBet extends. - @wang2024localgp Local Gaussian process extrapolation for BART models --- the alternative extrapolation strategy referenced by @wang2024longbet. - @callaway2021did and @roth2023trending for the econometric literature on staggered adoption that LongBet is positioned against. - @deng2013cuped for the variance-reduction idea that $\mu(X_i, t)$ generalizes. :::
